title: The Nine O’Clock Sheet and Half a Roll of Green Labels
teaser: The seven exhibition stands under Zhou Hang’s responsibility must be finished early, but the critical power points clients will use also have to be checked one by one before the panels are closed. A new bonus rewards only the number of stands finished by nine, while available site time stays the same, so a reasonable push for earlier completion begins to change where he spends that time.
paragraphs: At 6:10 in the evening, Zhou Hang crouched beside the back wall of stand five with a roll of green labels in his hand. Every time he confirmed a socket the client would use, he placed one label on the drawing and another on the cable; only after that check did the carpenter close the final section of skirting. He had worked this way during the previous two exhibitions, completing the electrical checks as the stand was built. On temporary stands, it was not unusual for wiring, numbering, or the equipment list to disagree. When such differences were found before the panels were closed, they usually took only a few minutes to correct. That evening he was responsible for seven stands and, besides the power checks, had to release the installation of lightboxes, cabinets, and finishes.

At 6:25, the project group posted a new bonus rule: the more stands completed before nine the next morning, the higher the site bonus. At the previous show, an early-arriving client had still found workers finishing up, so the company wanted to improve morning completion. The requirement itself was not unreasonable. When the message appeared, the electrician at stand five was waiting for Zhou Hang to continue the circuit checks, while four workers at stand six were also waiting for his approval before they could lift the lightbox. Under his old sequence, he would have finished checking the remaining circuits at stand five first. This time he looked at the clock, put the roll of green labels back in the tool cart, and went to release the work at stand six.

Nothing went wrong immediately that evening. After eight, Zhou Hang returned to stand five and finished the checks, finding only one number that needed correction. Early the next morning, he kept the same priority: whenever his signature could let a work crew continue immediately, he handled that first; electrical verification that did not block construction was moved into the gaps. Cabinets, finishes, and lightboxes were still inspected against the original checklist. No standard was removed. At exactly nine, six of the seven stands were complete, a completion rate of about 86 percent; at the previous exhibition, five had been complete at the same time, about 71 percent. The roll of green labels in the tool cart had been used only about half as much as it normally would have been by that point.

At eleven, the client at stand eight connected a sample refrigerator to the reserved socket on the right wall according to the equipment drawing confirmed a week earlier. The final load verification had not yet been done. When the electrician checked it, he found that one on-site circuit number had been matched to the wrong point on the drawing. The line had not suddenly failed, and the client had not changed the equipment location; this was exactly the kind of ordinary discrepancy the point-by-point check was meant to catch before the panels were closed. To reach the junction box, the carpenter removed a short section of newly installed skirting, the electrician adjusted and relabeled the circuit, and the carpenter installed it again. Two people who had been about to finish work at stand ten spent another forty minutes there instead, while the client’s display cart had to wait in the aisle.

At 1:40 p.m., another already-closed cabinet had to be opened because the equipment list and the on-site labels had not yet been fully reconciled, adding another forty-five minutes from start to finish. Zhou Hang located the issue quickly when he performed the delayed check, showing that his judgment and execution had not deteriorated. At the previous exhibition, under similar time pressure, the checks had also uncovered two numbering mismatches. But because the green-label verification had then moved with the build, both were corrected before the panels were closed and did not become rework. Finishing early was still a reasonable objective. What had changed was that, within the same limited site time, only “completed before nine” was tied to the bonus.

The final review sheet contained two sets of numbers, both true. The completion rate before nine had risen from about 71 percent to about 86 percent, and the number of failures in the construction-quality inspection had not increased. Another column now recorded two panel reopenings, eighty-five minutes of additional labor, and two periods of client waiting. No one proposed removing the nine o’clock target, because clients genuinely wanted to see complete stands early in the morning. After the meeting, Zhou Hang handed the nine o’clock sheet to the project manager. The six completed stands had already been counted toward the bonus. He pushed the cart back to the warehouse and placed the remaining roll of green labels in a drawer, with half the roll still wound around the core.
explanation: Strategic control is not only about setting goals. It also requires the critical activities employees are expected to perform, the performance measures, and the rewards to support the overall result together. When several necessary tasks compete for the same time but rewards cover only one easily counted outcome, employees can rationally raise the relative priority of the rewarded task even when their capability, sense of responsibility, and quality standards remain unchanged. The rewarded metric may improve, while necessary but unrewarded work is delayed, causing problems to surface later and increasing total delivery cost or harming the client outcome.
mapping: Before the bonus rule, Zhou Hang completes the electrical checks in parallel with construction, so ordinary discrepancies are found before the panels are closed → This establishes the normal baseline and shows that the green-label check is an established and valuable part of delivery.

After the new bonus counts only the number of stands completed before nine, he first handles approvals that immediately release construction crews → The same person reallocates limited time because of the reward structure, not because the client requirements or his capability change.

Completion before nine rises from 5/7 to 6/7, while all cabinet, finish, and lightbox checks still take place → The rewarded measure genuinely improves, and the story does not artificially remove high quality standards.

Ordinary verification discrepancies that would previously have been found before panel closure surface only after the clients arrive, producing two reopenings and 85 minutes of extra work → The reward does not create the wiring discrepancies; it changes when they are discovered and resolved, making their consequences larger.
boundary: A single-output reward is not inherently harmful. If tasks are independent and do not compete for the same time or attention, or if quality, risk, and other critical outcomes are already protected by reliable hard constraints, concentrating rewards on one output can be very effective. This mechanism mainly appears when several necessary tasks share limited resources while measurement and rewards cover only some of them. Even when rework appears, correlation alone is not enough to conclude that the incentive caused it; the tasks, people, and conditions before and after the rule change still need to be compared.
reflection: If completion before nine must remain a target, how could the bonus sheet also protect the green-label work that has to be finished before the panels are closed but is harder to count?
